section_summary: This section chiefly documents the 1934 controversy over the Marcus Show, whose American performers entered Japan on short-term transit visas and were compelled to depart after Japanese authorities refused a further extension. The correspondence examines erroneous visa-fee advice by the Japanese Consulate General at San Francisco, the reciprocal visa-fee waiver, and political and cultural opposition to the revue in Japan; it also covers a retired naval officer’s visa complaint and the refusal to let an American Justice Department official land at Yokohama without a passport. The final pages contain later file-circulation slips and a 1930 consular report on Japan’s state-supported development of foreign tourism.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy reply concerning the Marcus Show visas
subfiles.to: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports that the Marcus Show’s visa difficulty resulted from a misunderstanding by the Japanese Consul General at San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: Saito replies to Phillips’s May 24 inquiry about the theatrical troupe compelled to leave Japan after an eighteen-day extension. He states that an investigation found the Consul General had misunderstood the 1926 reciprocal visa-waiver agreement. He expresses regret and says the consul was instructed to exercise greater care.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum concerning the delayed Japanese reply
subfiles.about: Records an inquiry to Japanese Embassy official Tsuchiya about a reply to Phillips’s May 24 letter.
subfiles.summary: A State Department official telephoned Tsuchiya at the Japanese Embassy to ask when a response to Phillips’s May 24 communication could be expected. Tsuchiya apologized for the delay and indicated that the Embassy would pursue the matter with San Francisco.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Thomas on the Marcus Show case
subfiles.about: Explains the Department’s understanding of the Marcus Show visa dispute and its efforts to obtain a Japanese response.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges correspondence from George D. Pyper concerning the American revue company’s difficulties in Japan. It explains that the troupe received transit rather than entry visas and that the Embassy in Tokyo worked toward an amicable adjustment. The Department had raised aspects of the case with the Japanese Embassy and promised to report further developments.

subfiles.title: Recommendation for reply and confidential telephone briefing to Senator Thomas
subfiles.about: Suggests sending the attached draft reply and privately briefing Senator Thomas from Ambassador Grew’s despatch.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recommends that Hornbeck sign the proposed response to Senator Thomas. It also suggests informing the senator confidentially of the sensitive portions of Grew’s April 19 despatch concerning obstacles to an amicable settlement.

subfiles.title: Senator Thomas requests advice on replying to George D. Pyper
subfiles.about: Asks Hornbeck for guidance on answering confidential correspondence from George D. Pyper.
subfiles.summary: Thomas forwards confidential letters and asks Hornbeck for suggestions about what he should tell Pyper or do on the matter. He requests that the correspondence be returned after review.

subfiles.title: George D. Pyper forwards the Marcus Company correspondence
subfiles.about: Requests assistance for Ned Alvord and the Marcus Company after its exclusion from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Pyper encloses correspondence received from Ned Alvord, then in Shanghai. He asks whether anything can be done to enable the company to return to Japan and fulfill its contracted engagements.

subfiles.title: Ned Alvord’s cover letter to George D. Pyper
subfiles.about: Asks Pyper to pass an attached account of the Marcus Show dispute to influential persons in Washington.
subfiles.summary: Alvord describes the attached statement as conservative and accurate and asks Pyper to place it where it might have influence. He contrasts Japan’s treatment of the American troupe with opportunities long afforded Japanese performers in the United States. He also says he waited until reaching Shanghai because he feared Japanese postal surveillance and loss of critical mail.

subfiles.title: Ned Alvord’s account of the Marcus Show’s removal from Japan to George D. Pyper
subfiles.about: Describes the refusal to extend the Marcus Show’s Japanese visas and alleges discrimination against its American members.
subfiles.summary: Alvord says the Japanese consular office in San Francisco had assured Charles Hugo that the troupe’s initial four-week permission could be extended in Japan. Despite the show’s successful Tokyo engagement, guarantees offered by theatrical and shipping interests, and tentative bookings in Nagoya and Osaka, the Home Office refused another extension. He praises Ambassador Grew’s assistance, speculates about commercial or anti-American motives, and asks that responsible authorities take notice.

subfiles.title: Passport Division reply to Hardie Meakin
subfiles.about: Advises that the Department has raised the Marcus Show matter with the Japanese Ambassador.
subfiles.summary: Shipley acknowledges Meakin’s June 6 letter to Frank E. Duvall. He states that the issue has been taken up with the Japanese Ambassador and promises another communication once a reply is received.

subfiles.title: Hardie Meakin forwards Ned Alvord’s complaint
subfiles.about: Requests investigation and possible reconsideration of Japan’s refusal to readmit the Marcus Show.
subfiles.summary: Meakin encloses a letter from Ned Alvord and suggests that the show may have suffered because it was too successful. Acting at David M. Idzal’s request, he asks why the extension was refused and whether the Japanese Government might allow the company to return for its planned engagements.

subfiles.title: Ned Alvord’s account of the Marcus Show dispute to David M. Idzal
subfiles.about: Gives a detailed account of the visa-extension refusal and asks that American businesspeople be informed.
subfiles.summary: Alvord says the troupe accepted time-limited visas after being assured that extensions could be arranged in Japan. He describes the profitable Tokyo engagement, proposed Nagoya and Osaka bookings, bond offers, and the Home Office’s refusal to permit a longer stay. He characterizes the decision as discriminatory and speculates about commercial rivalry or official anti-American sentiment.

subfiles.title: Passport Division reply to Representative Boehne
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Boehne’s Marcus Show correspondence and reports that the Japanese Ambassador has been approached.
subfiles.summary: Shipley acknowledges Boehne’s May 24 letter concerning the troupe’s stay in Japan. He promises to communicate again when the Japanese Ambassador replies.

subfiles.title: Representative Boehne forwards the Marcus Show protest
subfiles.about: Transmits correspondence protesting Japan’s refusal to extend the Marcus Show’s stay.
subfiles.summary: Boehne describes the troupe as playing to capacity audiences in Japan. He forwards its protest to the Secretary of State for comment and any action deemed appropriate.

subfiles.title: Marce E. Bowen forwards Alvord’s letter to Representative Boehne
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of Ned Alvord’s account of the Marcus Show situation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bowen identifies Alvord as an experienced theatrical producer and sends his letter at Charlie Atkins’s request. He says he knows nothing independently about the Japanese situation and has also sent a copy to Senator Van Nuys.

subfiles.title: Ned Alvord’s account of the Marcus Show dispute to Marce Bowen
subfiles.about: Describes the visa dispute and asks Bowen to inform American business contacts.
subfiles.summary: Alvord recounts assurances allegedly given in San Francisco, the troupe’s successful Tokyo engagement, and the Home Office’s refusal to authorize later bookings in Nagoya and Osaka. He says guarantees and cash deposits were offered without success and calls the action discriminatory. He also cites Ambassador Grew’s assistance and press speculation that the show’s success provoked opposition.

subfiles.title: Ned Alvord’s cover note to Marce Bowen
subfiles.about: Asks Bowen to circulate the attached Marcus Show statement after Alvord’s arrival in Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Alvord calls the attached account a conservative statement of the facts and requests help placing it before influential people. He compares the treatment of American and Japanese performers and criticizes Japanese policy. He adds that fear of postal surveillance caused him to delay writing until he reached Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Passport Division reply to Sol Bloom
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese Ambassador is being consulted about Ned Alvord’s complaint.
subfiles.summary: Shipley acknowledges Bloom’s May 22 communication enclosing Alvord’s April 30 letter from Shanghai. He states that the Department is taking the Marcus Show case up with the Japanese Ambassador and will communicate again upon receiving a response.

subfiles.title: Sol Bloom forwards Ned Alvord’s letter
subfiles.about: Transmits a letter for the Secretary of State’s consideration.
subfiles.summary: Bloom sends the Department a letter he received that day. The enclosure is Alvord’s detailed account of the Marcus Show controversy.

subfiles.title: Ned Alvord’s report on the Marcus Show incident to Sol Bloom
subfiles.about: Presents an expanded allegation that Japanese technical, political, and ideological opposition forced the Marcus Show to leave.
subfiles.summary: Alvord describes the visa assurances received in San Francisco, the successful Tokyo engagement, and the rejection of further engagements in Nagoya and Osaka. He alleges discrimination and reports a theory that militarist groups opposed the revue because entertainment distracted the public during a proclaimed national emergency. He also contrasts Japan’s treatment of the troupe with American opportunities for Japanese performers and alleges that Japanese officials inspected or suppressed critical mail.

subfiles.title: William Phillips’s inquiry to the Japanese Ambassador
subfiles.about: Asks whether the Marcus Show’s difficulty arose from misunderstanding the 1926 reciprocal visa-waiver agreement.
subfiles.summary: Phillips recounts that the sixty performers were quoted ten dollars each for temporary visitor visas and consequently accepted free transit visas limited to one month. After an eighteen-day extension they were required to leave Japan before completing their engagements. He asks whether the Japanese Consulate General at San Francisco misunderstood the bilateral fee-waiver arrangement.

subfiles.title: Passport Division routing note on the proposed Japanese communication
subfiles.about: Routes the proposed visa communication for review against the file and waiver agreement.
subfiles.summary: The partly illegible note concerns the form of a communication to the Japanese Embassy. It directs attention to the relevant file and the reciprocal visa-fee waiver.

subfiles.title: Passport Division memorandum to Miss Alexander
subfiles.about: Requests advice on whether the proposed note should go to Far Eastern Affairs or be redrafted.
subfiles.summary: The writer asks whether the communication should be sent to the Far Eastern Division for comment or recast in the form of an earlier note. The memorandum considers the Japanese Consulate General apparently at fault and regards the proposed note as appropriate.

subfiles.title: Handwritten recommendation for an informal communication
subfiles.about: Recommends handling the Japanese visa inquiry informally after reviewing the flagged file.
subfiles.summary: The brief handwritten response refers to the marked file. It concludes that the communication should be made on an informal basis.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on evidentiary basis and diplomatic form
subfiles.to: Passport Division and Under Secretary’s office
subfiles.about: Advises against formally blaming the Japanese Consulate General and recommends an informal inquiry.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum finds insufficient evidence to attribute the original visa error officially to the Japanese Consulate General at San Francisco. It recommends an informal letter from the Under Secretary to the Japanese Ambassador describing the troupe’s difficulty and asking whether the 1926 reciprocal agreement had been misunderstood.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 749: Marcus Show
subfiles.about: Explains the technical and political causes of the Marcus Show’s removal from Japan and recommends reciprocal visa treatment.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards the troupe manager’s appeal, the Embassy’s answer, and a shipping-company telegram confirming the visa arrangements. He confidentially reports opposition from reactionary societies and influential older Japanese friends of America, as well as Foreign Office fears that an incident might damage bilateral relations. He describes unsuccessful informal efforts by Embassy personnel and Shigeru Yoshida and concludes that the San Francisco consulate apparently erred in attempting to charge visa fees waived under the 1926 agreement.

subfiles.title: Charles Hugo’s appeal to Ambassador Grew
subfiles.about: Requests Embassy intervention so the Marcus Show can obtain visa extensions and fulfill its Japanese contracts.
subfiles.summary: Hugo says he was told in San Francisco that the troupe could obtain extensions in Japan after receiving thirty-day visas. The refusal of another extension threatened contracted performances through May 27, a forty-five-day idle period, severe expense, and possibly abandonment of the tour. He presents the venture as a goodwill exchange and asks Grew to persuade the authorities to reconsider.

subfiles.title: Embassy reply to Charles Hugo
subfiles.from: Erle R. Dickover, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: Explains why the Embassy cannot obtain further Japanese visa extensions for the Marcus Show.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reconstructs how the troupe received thirty-day transit visas, was eventually permitted to perform, and obtained an eighteen-day extension before a final departure order. Officials believed the case might have been resolved had negotiations begun before the Home Affairs order, but rescinding that order was considered nearly impossible. A proposed trip to Shanghai for new visas was abandoned because of additional sensitive considerations, although Japanese officials acknowledged the troupe’s exemplary conduct.

subfiles.title: Nippon Yusen Kaisha telegram on the Marcus Show visas
subfiles.from: Nippon Yusen Kaisha office, San Francisco
subfiles.to: Nippon Yusen Kaisha head office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Confirms that the troupe accepted free thirty-day transit visas because it could not pay visa fees.
subfiles.summary: The telegram says the party lacked funds for the quoted visa fees and had not specified its exact intended stay. Transit visas were therefore granted for thirty days on the understanding that Hugo would arrange any necessary extension in Japan. It adds that the Japanese Consulate at San Francisco had informed the Foreign Ministry of the circumstances.

subfiles.title: Navy Department report on Frederic N. Pugsley’s Japanese visa complaint
subfiles.about: Forwards a report that the Japanese Consulate at San Francisco demanded visa fees from a retired naval officer and his family.
subfiles.summary: Pugsley reported that the consulate required ten dollars per person for visas valid longer than seven days, despite allegedly issuing longer free visas to civilian tourists. He believed that his status as a retired naval officer might have led the consulate to deny a longer stay even if he paid.

subfiles.title: Visa Office memorandum on the 1926 Japanese visa-fee agreement
subfiles.about: Summarizes the legal basis and coverage of the reciprocal Japanese-American visa-fee waiver.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum cites the Act of February 25, 1925, and Executive Order of May 15, 1935. It states that the Tokyo Embassy concluded an agreement effective July 10, 1926, waiving visa and application fees for temporary visitors, travelers in transit, and qualifying traders.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning Frederic N. Pugsley
subfiles.about: Explains the visa-fee waiver but declines to challenge Japan’s authority to limit Pugsley’s permitted stay.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that the 1926 agreement appears to make the requested fees improper. Because Pugsley had abandoned his trip, it saw no need to approach Japanese authorities about his individual case. It adds that international law permits a sovereign state to exclude foreigners or impose conditions on entry, so representations could address an improper fee but not the duration of an American visitor’s stay.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on landing Japanese travelers without passports
subfiles.about: Suggests examining U.S. practice concerning Japanese travelers without passports before disposing of the Smith case.
subfiles.summary: The note raises the question whether U.S. immigration authorities allow Japanese persons without passports to go ashore. It recommends considering that practice in determining where the associated case belongs.

subfiles.title: Refusal of Japanese Authorities to Permit American Official to Land at Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports the refusal to let J. W. B. Smith land at Yokohama because he lacked a passport.
subfiles.summary: Smith, traveling to Manila aboard the President Coolidge, carried only a Justice Department appointment letter bearing Japanese and Chinese visas. Japanese harbor police declined to treat it as a passport because it contained no citizenship statement, description, or photograph. Smith’s assertion that he was traveling under an assumed name on a secret mission provided a possible additional reason for the refusal, which Boyce regarded as understandable.

subfiles.title: Appointment and travel authorization for J. W. B. Smith
subfiles.from: Joseph B. Keenan, for the Attorney General
subfiles.about: Authorizes Smith to travel to the Philippines in connection with drafting its proposed constitution.
subfiles.summary: The letter identifies Smith as a Special Assistant to the Attorney General assigned to work connected with the proposed Philippine constitution and independence legislation. It authorizes necessary travel and specifies transportation reimbursement and a five-dollar daily allowance. Notes record Japanese and Chinese visas issued in Honolulu on August 15.

subfiles.summary: The slip’s heading identifies file 894.111 and an OCR-corrupted form of Tigner’s name. The remaining handwritten date and routing notation are too uncertain to normalize reliably.

subfiles.title: Organization of Japanese Tourist Trade on an Industrial Basis and Creation of a Control Organization in the Department of Railways—incomplete duplicate
subfiles.about: Introduces Japan’s effort to develop tourism as part of national economic recovery and trade-balance policy.
subfiles.summary: The title page identifies a Tokyo consular report approved by Consul General Arthur Garrels. Its surviving second page explains that the Hamaguchi Cabinet linked economic retrenchment, lifting the gold embargo, and improvement of the trade balance. A government commission consequently recommended official machinery and a public advisory body to promote foreign tourism.

subfiles.title: Organization of Japanese Tourist Trade on an Industrial Basis and Creation of a Control Organization in the Department of Railways
subfiles.about: Analyzes the organization, financing, advertising, and economic objectives of Japan’s state-supported foreign-tourism industry.
subfiles.summary: The report traces tourism promotion from the Honored-Guest Association through the Japan Tourist Bureau and the newly created Board and Commission of Tourist Industry. It describes guidebook publication, travel services, hotel cooperation, overseas offices, American magazine advertising, familiarization tours, loans for hotel improvements, guide regulation, national parks, and preservation of scenic attractions. Tourism is presented as a means to improve Japan’s balance of payments by attracting more visitors—especially Americans—and lengthening their stays. The report concludes with visitor statistics, financial data, enclosure references, and a list of government, bureau, press, and interview sources.
